passages.happening:
Psalm 1 does not speak to God. It speaks to the reader, like a teacher at the door of a house. It opens, “Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, or set foot on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of mockers” (verse 1).

Then comes the turn: “But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night” (verse 2).

And then a picture: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and who prospers in all he does” (verse 3).

So the first half of the psalm moves in three steps. What this person turns away from. What he loves instead. What his life becomes.
passages.hearers:
‘Blessed’ here is the Hebrew word ashre. It is not quite the word used when a priest blesses someone or when people bless God. That is a different Hebrew word. Ashre is more like a cry of wonder at someone: how happy, how well off, what a good life. It is said of people, never of God. It describes a life that is going well in the deepest sense, a life anyone would wish for. Some Bibles print ‘happy’; the Berean Standard Bible keeps ‘blessed’. Neither English word quite catches it, which is why both are used.

This site usually avoids ‘blessed’ as an easy word for anything nice. Here it is the Bible's own word, and it means something weighty.

Notice the three steps in verse 1: walk, set foot (stand), sit. A person walks past bad advice, then stops on the path, then sits down and stays among those who mock what is good. The psalm shows how drifting becomes settling.

‘Law’ is the Hebrew torah. It means more than rules. It means God's teaching, his instruction for life. A person ‘delights’ in it, the way one delights in a gift.

‘Meditates’ is a Hebrew verb that means to murmur, to say something quietly under your breath. In the ancient world people read aloud, even alone. To meditate on God's teaching was to say it over and over, softly, until it sank in.

The tree is not a wild tree that happened to grow by a river. ‘Planted’ means it was set there on purpose. The ‘streams’ are channels, the ditches farmers dug to carry water to their trees. In a dry land with a long, hot summer, such a tree stayed green when others dried up.
passages.later:
Joshua was told the same thing about God's teaching: “meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it” (Joshua 1:8).

Jeremiah uses almost the same picture: “But blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD” is “like a tree planted by the waters that sends out its roots toward the stream” (Jeremiah 17:7-8). Scholars debate whether one of these passages borrowed from the other, or both drew on a common saying.

Jesus begins his teaching in Matthew with the same kind of saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3). He also judged a life by its fruit: “every good tree bears good fruit” (Matthew 7:17).

Many Christians, from early times, have seen in the person of Psalm 1 a picture that only Jesus fully lived: a life wholly shaped by God's word.
passages.hard:
Does this psalm promise that good people always do well? Verse 3 says the righteous person “prospers in all he does.” Read alone, that sounds like a guarantee: be good, and life will go well.

But the book of Psalms itself refuses that reading. In Psalm 73 a faithful man almost loses his footing: “For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked” (73:3). Many laments cry out that the righteous suffer while the wicked thrive. The book of Job argues the point at length. Job asks, “Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?” (Job 21:7), and God does not tell him he is wrong to ask.

So readers take verse 3 in more than one way. Some read it as a general truth of wisdom, true over a whole life but not in every case, like a proverb. Some read ‘prospers’ as inner fruitfulness, a life rooted in God, which can go on even through loss. Some read the psalm as looking to God's final judgment, when the two ways will be clearly seen. Many hold all three together.

Notice one small word: the tree yields its fruit “in season.” Not on demand, and not every month. Psalm 1 does not promise success on a human timetable.
passages.asks:
Look at the three verbs again: walk, stand, sit. Ask where you are drifting, and where drifting has already become sitting.

Then ask what you are rooted near. The psalm does not tell you to try harder. It tells you to stay close to the water. One simple way: read a few lines of Scripture slowly, out loud, and return to them during the day.

passages.happening:
The second half begins sharply: “Not so the wicked! For they are like chaff driven off by the wind” (verse 4).

Then comes the outcome: “Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous” (verse 5).

And the reason for everything: “For the LORD guards the path of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish” (verse 6). The psalm ends on that last word.
passages.hearers:
Every first hearer had seen chaff. After the harvest, grain was beaten or trampled on a hard, flat place called a threshing floor. Then, on a windy day, farmers tossed it into the air with a wooden fork. The heavy grain fell back down. The light husks, the chaff, blew away.

Set the two pictures side by side. The tree is rooted, heavy with fruit, green in the heat. The chaff has no root and no weight. Nothing holds it. The wind decides where it goes.

‘Will not stand in the judgment’ may mean God's final verdict on a life. It may also recall the gathering of God's people, the ‘assembly’, where a person had to stand and be counted. Readers take it both ways.

‘Guards’ in verse 6 is the Hebrew word ‘knows’. In Hebrew, to know often means more than to have facts about something. It means to care for it, to be close to it. The LORD knows the way of the righteous: he watches it, he keeps it.

The psalm's first word in Hebrew is ‘blessed’ (ashre). Its last word is ‘will perish’. Between those two words lie two ways to live.
passages.later:
Moses set the same choice before Israel: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19). Jeremiah repeats it: “I set before you the way of life and the way of death” (Jeremiah 21:8).

John the Baptist used the picture of the threshing floor for the judgment Jesus would bring. He will “gather His wheat into the barn”, John said, but “He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matthew 3:12).

Jesus spoke of two ways too: a wide road that leads to destruction and a narrow one that leads to life (Matthew 7:13-14).

Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 belong together. Psalm 1 opens with ‘blessed’ and Psalm 2 ends with it (2:12). The Talmud records that some early rabbis counted them as one psalm. Some early Christian copies of Acts call Psalm 2 ‘the first psalm’ (at Acts 13:33), which suggests the same habit.
passages.asks:
The psalm leaves you with two pictures, a tree and chaff, and does not let you stand between them. It asks which one your life is becoming.

It also offers comfort, not only warning. The LORD knows your way. If you are trying to walk toward him, you are not walking alone or unseen.
